title: The Year Shibusawa Eiichi Left the Finance Ministry to Run a Bank
dek: In 1873 a senior Japanese finance official resigned to run the country's first national bank, a venture its own merchant backers barely wanted.

story.company: First National Bank (Dai-Ichi Kokuritsu Ginko, later Dai-Ichi Bank and Mizuho Bank)
story.event: Resigning from the Ministry of Finance to become superintendent of the newly formed First National Bank
story.summary: In 1873 Shibusawa Eiichi, a senior Ministry of Finance official who had drafted Japan's National Bank Act, resigned from government and became superintendent of the First National Bank (Dai-Ichi Kokuritsu Ginko), a joint venture of the reluctant Mitsui and Ono merchant houses whose public share offering sold poorly. After the Ono house failed in 1874-75 and the government withdrew its deposits, he cut capital and closed branches; the bank survived and he led it until 1916.
paragraphs: In 1873 Shibusawa Eiichi was 33 and a senior official in Japan's Ministry of Finance. The son of an indigo-dealing farming family, he had joined the Meiji government in 1869, worked in its Reform Office alongside Ōkuma Shigenobu, Itō Hirobumi and Inoue Kaoru on railways, telegraphs, the post, banks and joint-stock companies, and drafted the National Bank Act of December 1872, which let licensed private banks issue notes on the American model.

He also carried a lesson from Paris, where in 1867 he kept the accounts for Tokugawa Akitake's delegation to the Exposition. Watching the banker Paul Flury-Hérard handle military business there, Japan's National Diet Library says, convinced him that Japan's status order had to go and that business people deserved higher standing. Inside government, a Meiji University historian writes, he decided he could not do what he wanted; a business historian says he was caught up in political manoeuvring. That year he resigned, in the words of a Japanese government profile, to promote private-sector business.

He took a post outside government: sōkan-yaku, or superintendent, of the First National Bank (Dai-Ichi Kokuritsu Ginkō), the first bank formed under the new law. Despite its name it ran on private money. It opened in 1873 in a Western-style building at Kaiunbashi in Tokyo that the government made the Mitsui house hand over. The bank joined two great merchant houses, Mitsui and Ono, at the government's urging, and Mitsui Bank's official history later called the venture a throwaway stone. Each house took a million yen of shares. Of the shares offered to the public, fewer than half sold, leaving 2,440,800 yen from 71 shareholders, according to a study of the bank's registers.

The first two years tested the bet. In 1874 the Ono house closed its doors amid a wider panic, and its shares, a third of the bank's capital, were lost. In 1875 the government said it would withdraw its deposits, about 70 per cent of the total in late 1873. Shibusawa cut the capital, closed branches and persuaded officials to withdraw the deposits over two years rather than at once. The bank survived. He became its president in 1875, by 1876 held its second-largest block of shares, and led it until 1916. Its line runs on into Mizuho Bank.

quote.text: Commerce is a game of skill, which every man cannot play, which few men can play well. The right merchant is one who has the just average of faculties we call common sense; a man of a strong affinity for facts, who makes up his decision on what he has seen.
quote.source_title: The Conduct of Life, Project Gutenberg eBook #39827
quote.connection: Shibusawa left office convinced that business deserved the respect Japan gave its officials. Emerson, writing in 1860, likewise treated commerce as a demanding skill grounded in facts, not luck. Shibusawa's first two years at the bank, spent on one hard fact after another, put exactly that skill to the test.

reflection: Leaving a respected post rarely feels brave from the inside. For Shibusawa it meant a title outside government, partners who did not want to be there, and a bank that lost a third of its capital in its second year. What carried him was not applause but a settled view that the work mattered, and the patience to meet one crisis at a time.

You may feel the pull of how others rank your work: a title, a salary, what relatives say when they ask what you do these days. That pull is real and worth naming. It is a poor guide to whether the work is worth doing, and a poorer one still at the end of a tiring day.
invitation: Think of one person whose opinion of your work weighs on you. Write one sentence saying what you would want them to understand about it, and keep that sentence for yourself today.

cross_checks.claim: Shibusawa resigned from the Ministry of Finance in 1873 and became superintendent (sokan-yaku) of the First National Bank
He left because he could not do what he wanted inside government and wished to promote private business, amid political manoeuvring
Shibusawa helped design the national bank system of 1872, modelled on the American system
The First National Bank opened in 1873 under the 1872 national bank law, in the former Mitsui-gumi building at Kaiunbashi
The Ono house failed (closing its doors in 1874; removed from the bank's register by 1875)

research_notes: Reasons for leaving: sources describe them differently. Sasaki (Meiji University) says he decided he could not do what he wanted inside government; Shimada (business historian) says he was caught up in political manoeuvring; the Japanese government's KIZUNA profile says he resigned to promote private-sector business; Wikipedia-derived pages speak of a policy or factional dispute and link his departure to Inoue Kaoru's. Without access to his autobiography the story gives these as attributed views and does not name a budget quarrel or quote Shibusawa. Date of the Ono failure: the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says the Ono and Shimada houses closed their doors in 1874; Kahm's dissertation dates the Ono bankruptcy to 1875 (its shares leaving the register in August 1875). The story says the house closed its doors in 1874 and its shares were lost, without dating the formal bankruptcy. Capital figures (planned 3 million yen; Mitsui and Ono 1 million each; 4,408 public shares sold; 2,440,800 yen; 71 shareholders), the 70 per cent share of government deposits, the 'throwaway stone' phrase, the two-year withdrawal and his 1876 shareholding rest on Kahm's dissertation, which cites Kato and Ouchi (1963) and Tamaki (1995); the page is blocked for automated checks (403) though it loaded for the researcher, so these figures are single-sourced and attributed in the story to 'a study of the bank's registers'. Kahm's own text gives Shibusawa 500 shares at founding while its table shows 400, so the story gives no founding shareholding. Kahm writes that capital was reduced 'by 1.5 million yen' while his table shows shares falling from 25,000 to 15,000 (to 1.5 million yen), so the story says only that he cut the capital. Shimada gives his age at leaving the presidency in 1916 as 77 (traditional reckoning); the story gives no age. The KIZUNA profile gives his age at resignation as 33, which fits his birth in February 1840. The J-STAGE PDF of Shimada's article loads but its embedded text is partly unreadable to the checker. Titles: the Foundation's chronology calls his first post sokan-yaku (superintendent) and dates the presidency to 1875; some sources loosely call him president from 1873.
